key_insight: EEG foundation models can look strong or weak depending on dataset identity, split strategy, and control baselines, so transfer claims need stress-testing.
clinical_relevance: For clinical EEG decoding, frozen pretrained representations may not outperform classical features or even random encoders, except in some cross-subject tasks like ictal detection.
method: Benchmarked 6 pretrained EEG models across 5 clinical tasks and 4 datasets.
Used frozen linear probes with leave-one-subject-out, subject-grouped, or recording-level splits.
Ran targeted controls: random initialization, random features, label permutation, scrambled-label fine-tuning, and projection tests.
evidence_signal: Dataset identity was decoded almost perfectly from embeddings (AUROC 1.000 at PCA-50; 0.9998 after preprocessing), while Korean diagnosis decoding was far lower (0.528) and CHB-MIT ictal detection was the clearest positive result (0.793 AUROC).
watch_item: Performance is highly sensitive to evaluation unit and comparator choice, so results from frozen probes may not generalize without patient-disjoint validation and strong negative controls.
paper_title: Stress-Testing EEG Foundation Models for Clinical Decoding: Dataset Identity and Targeted Negative Controls
